prompt: `pgbench -c 8 -j 4 -T 30 bench` reports 3980 tps, and lesson 2's workload on the same machine runs at about a third of that. Which is the server's real speed?
hint: A benchmark measures a server running something.

choices.text: 3980, since the built-in test is the standard
choices.why: It is a standard workload, not yours; its number says nothing about the marketplace.

choices.text: Both, each for its own workload
choices.why: Right: a benchmark measures a server running a workload, never a server alone.

choices.text: The lower one, because it is the slowest case
choices.why: Neither is a worst case; they answer different questions.

choices.text: Their average, about 2600
choices.why: Averaging two workloads describes neither.

prompt: Why does the built-in test at `-s 10` partly measure lock waits rather than the server's speed?
hint: Count the rows in pgbench_branches.

choices.text: Every transaction hits one of ten rows
choices.why: Right: ten branch rows for eight clients; the scale sets how many, and the contention with it.

choices.text: pgbench takes a table lock before each run
choices.why: It runs ordinary statements; the waits come from row locks on hot rows.

choices.text: `-i` leaves the tables without primary keys
choices.why: The init output ends with `creating primary keys...`.

choices.text: It runs VACUUM on the tables during the test
choices.why: It vacuums once before starting, not during.

prompt: A colleague adds an index on `orders(status)` and reruns `pgbench -c 8 -T 30 bench` to see if the shop got faster. What will the number tell them?
hint: Which tables does the built-in test touch?

choices.text: Whether the pending count got faster
choices.why: The built-in test never queries orders.

choices.text: How much the index slows the writes down
choices.why: Its writes go to pgbench_ tables, which the index is not on.

choices.text: Whether the index was built correctly
choices.why: A benchmark cannot check an index it never uses.

choices.text: Nothing: it runs on its own tables
choices.why: Right: it runs in bench, on pgbench_ tables; only the shop's workload can show the index.

prompt: Where should a benchmark's script weights come from?
hint: Something the server already counts.

choices.text: From the call counts of pg_stat_statements at a busy hour
choices.why: Right: each script's share of the calls is its weight.

choices.text: Equal weights, to be fair to every script
choices.why: Fairness is not the goal; the real mix is.

choices.text: From total_exec_time, so that slow statements count for more
choices.why: Time is the result to measure, not the mix to reproduce.

choices.text: From what the developers expect
choices.why: Lesson 2's weights were that kind of guess.

prompt: Why does `weights.sql` count `place-order.sql` through its first `INSERT` only?
hint: How many statements does one purchase send?

choices.text: The UPDATE is not recorded by pg_stat_statements
choices.why: It is recorded; lesson 2's tally listed it.

choices.text: INSERTs are the slowest statement in the script
choices.why: The COMMIT took most of the time; speed is not the reason.

choices.text: One purchase would count several times
choices.why: Right: one statement per script, so each transaction counts once.

choices.text: BEGIN and COMMIT belong to another script
choices.why: They belong to the same purchase.

prompt: The seller dashboard ran at 887 tps with `random(2, 1000)` and at 525 tps with `random_zipfian(1, 1000, 1.07)`. What changed?
hint: The SQL is identical.

choices.text: Zipfian sampling costs more processor time in pgbench
choices.why: The \set lines cost a thousandth of a millisecond.

choices.text: Which sellers were asked about
choices.why: Right: the big seller, now asked often, has far more December rows to count.

choices.text: The second run was cold
choices.why: Both ran back to back on a warm server.

choices.text: An index stopped being used
choices.why: Same statement, same indexes; the rows differ.

prompt: In a tally of one busy hour, a script's identifying statement has 6728 calls out of 66875 counted for all six scripts. What weight, in percent to one decimal, does it get?
hint: Its share of the calls.

prompt: Which line of a pgbench report should you check before trusting any of its other numbers?
hint: A run where transactions failed measured something else.

choices.text: `tps`
choices.why: Throughput of a run with failures counts work that was not your workload.

choices.text: `initial connection time`
choices.why: It is left out of tps and rarely matters.

choices.text: `number of failed transactions`
choices.why: Right: zero failures first, then read the rest.

choices.text: `scaling factor`
choices.why: For custom scripts it is just 1 and means nothing.

prompt: A run reports `latency average = 6.465 ms` and `latency stddev = 22.826 ms`. What does that say?
hint: Latency cannot go below zero.

choices.text: The measurement failed and should be thrown away
choices.why: It is a normal mixed workload; the numbers are right.

choices.text: A few slow ones pull the mean up
choices.why: Right: most are fast; the per-script blocks show 1 ms reads and a 198 ms count.

choices.text: Typical transactions take between 0 and 29 ms
choices.why: A symmetrical reading of the stddev does not fit a skewed spread.

choices.text: The server alternated between fast and slow seconds
choices.why: The progress lines moved by about 10%, not by a factor of three.

prompt: With `-r`, the purchase script shows `COMMIT` at 6.939 ms of its 9.368. Where does that time go?
hint: What must be true when COMMIT returns?

choices.text: Waiting for the record to reach disk
choices.why: Right: a commit waits for the write to be durable, and no index changes that.

choices.text: Into checking every foreign key again
choices.why: Foreign keys are checked by the INSERTs themselves here.

choices.text: Into pgbench's \set lines
choices.why: Those cost a thousandth of a millisecond each.

choices.text: Into rebuilding all the indexes on orders
choices.why: Indexes are updated during the INSERT, not rebuilt at commit.

prompt: The `pgbench` option that prints a line of throughput and latency every few seconds while the run is going is `-___`.
hint: Progress.

prompt: Why can a ten-second benchmark report a number that misleads?
hint: Compare with the progress lines.

choices.text: pgbench needs a minute to start all of its threads and clients
choices.why: Connections took 8.7 ms.

choices.text: Ten seconds is one progress interval, and those varied by 10%
choices.why: Right: it reports whichever interval it landed on, and misses the occasional checkpoint.

choices.text: Short runs are refused by the server
choices.why: Nothing refuses them; that is the trap.

choices.text: tps cannot be computed under thirty seconds
choices.why: It can; it is just less reliable.

prompt: `time pgbench … -T 30` on four processors printed `user 0m0.711s` and `sys 0m0.384s`. What percentage of the processor time available during the run did pgbench use, to one decimal?
hint: Available: 4 × 30 seconds.

prompt: Why do this course's benchmarks hardly ever touch the disk after the first minute?
hint: Compare two numbers from the sizes block.

choices.text: pgbench reads from a copy in its own memory
choices.why: pgbench sends SQL; the server reads the data.

choices.text: shared_buffers holds the whole database
choices.why: They are 128 MB; the OS cache does the holding.

choices.text: The data fits in free memory
choices.why: Right: 1352 MB against 14 GB; everything fits in the OS cache, which production larger than memory cannot do.

choices.text: The workload is read-only, so nothing is written
choices.why: place-order.sql writes every time it runs.

prompt: A closed-loop run reports 6.5 ms average latency at 1234 tps. The same workload at `-R 900` reports 17.1 ms with 13.0 ms of schedule lag. Which latency should a report about users quote, and why?
hint: Who waits when the server is busy?

choices.text: 6.5 ms, measured at the higher throughput
choices.why: The closed loop never sent the transactions that would have queued.

choices.text: 17.1 minus 13.0, the time actually spent in the server
choices.why: Users feel the wait for their turn too.

choices.text: Neither: only tps matters to users
choices.why: Users feel latency, not throughput.

choices.text: 17.1 ms: the wait counts for users
choices.why: Right: users arrive regardless, and a fixed rate counts the queue the closed loop hides.

prompt: Match each trap to the sign of it in a run.
hint: One sign each.

pairs.right: progress intervals that differ by as much as the change you are measuring
the first run of a series is the lowest
pgbench's own user and sys time
latency that falls when you offer more load

prompt: Three runs after a fresh copy gave 1157, 1434 and 1311 tps. Why is the 1157 thrown away?
hint: What had not happened yet before it?

choices.text: It is the lowest, and low results are pessimistic
choices.why: Discarding by value is choosing; it is discarded by position.

choices.text: It paid for warming a just-copied database
choices.why: Right: the first run of a series is a warm-up, whatever its number.

choices.text: pgbench's first run always includes the vacuum
choices.why: These runs used -n, no vacuum.

choices.text: The reset script was still running
choices.why: It had finished; its output was printed before the run.

prompt: After the warm-up, two runs gave 1311 and 1434 tps. A change then moves the number by 5%. What has been shown?
hint: Compare the change with the spread.

choices.text: A 5% improvement
choices.why: The same database moved by 9% between two runs.

choices.text: A 5% regression
choices.why: The direction is as unshown as the size.

choices.text: Nothing yet: 5% is inside a 9% noise
choices.why: Right: more or longer runs, or a bigger effect, are needed; lesson 24 decides.

choices.text: That the benchmark is broken
choices.why: Noise is normal; a benchmark without it would be suspicious.

prompt: Put the steps of a benchmark series in order.
hint: State first, numbers last.
items: Restore the data to a known state
Run the same command at least three times
Report the median and the range, with the command
trap: Reporting before the warm-up is discarded averages a cold run into the result.

prompt: Which of these make a benchmark more like production? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four lines a workload reproduces, and the traps.

choices.text: Weights from pg_stat_statements call counts
choices.why: Right: the real mix.

choices.text: Parameters drawn with the skew the data has
choices.why: Right: the dashboard dropped from 887 to 525 tps with it.

choices.text: A copy of the data the size of production
choices.why: Right: otherwise it measures a cached database.

choices.text: The built-in TPC-B-like test at a bigger scale
choices.why: A bigger bank is still a bank.

choices.text: The shortest run that gives a number
choices.why: Short runs report whichever interval they land on.

prompt: A team benchmarks a new server with lesson 2's workload: 10 seconds, one run, client on the server, a 2 GB copy of a 400 GB database. It reports 30% more tps than the old server. What is the strongest objection?
hint: Which trap changes what is being measured, not just how well?

choices.text: A 2 GB copy fits in memory; 400 GB does not
choices.why: Right: the disk that 400 GB needs was never measured. The others add noise; this one measures a different system.

choices.text: One run is noisy
choices.why: True, and a 30% gap might survive it; the copy's size cannot be repeated away.

choices.text: pgbench running on the server steals processor time
choices.why: Under one percent for this workload.

choices.text: Ten seconds misses checkpoints
choices.why: A real flaw, but smaller than measuring a cached database.
